description: I am a Master's student in Automation Engineering (Robotics) at the University of Vaasa, Finland. My interests include GNSS, satellite technology, robotics, AI, machine learning, and geospatial data analysis. I enjoy turning complex data into practical solutions. For this challenge, I am exploring MODIS–VIIRS satellite data harmonization to better understand global burning activity through data analytics, visualization, and anomaly detection. I am participating independently.
summary: FireScope is a web application that merges NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspots into one harmonised burning-activity record from 2000 to today. Raw hotspot counts can’t be compared over time: VIIRS (since 2012) has smaller pixels and detects about three times more fires than MODIS, so activity seems to jump when nothing changed on the ground. FireScope counts burning per place and day instead of per pixel, merges what both sensors saw without double counting, and uses the years when both satellites were flying to calibrate the MODIS-only years. Emergency managers, scientists, and land managers can pick any area and dates, see a colour-coded burning calendar, compare the current month with the area’s historical median, spot anomalies, and download CSV data and PDF reports. It turns 25 years of split satellite records into one fire history that can be trusted for planning and response.
details:
What it does
FireScope answers the challenge’s central question: when and where has an area burned, and is this month unusual? On a 3D globe, users see real MODIS and VIIRS detections, streamed in as they load. They select an area (country, coordinates, or a box drawn on the map) and dates. The Burning Calendar shows a year-by-month grid of harmonised fire activity on a colour-blind-friendly scale, with daily, weekly, yearly and seasonal views and a “this year vs historical median” chart. Anomaly Detection flags months and days that depart from the area’s own baseline for the same time of year. Reports & Export provides CSV hotspots with their harmonisation status, harmonised daily and monthly series, GeoJSON and a PDF report. Every export records the area, period and parameters.

How it works (harmonisation)

  1. One VIIRS satellite per day (S-NPP, then NOAA-20, then NOAA-21), so new satellites don’t inflate counts.
  2. Detections are placed on a 0.01° grid (about the MODIS pixel size) and counted as “active-fire cell-days”, so one fire covering many 375 m VIIRS pixels counts once.
  3. MODIS and VIIRS cell-days within 2 km on the same day are matched as the same burning, so nothing is counted twice.
  4. In each area’s 2012+ overlap, FireScope fits how MODIS-only counts relate to the combined record (a seasonal ratio with shrinkage, or a Theil–Sen fit) and applies it to 2000–2011. Uncertainty comes from leave-one-year-out cross-validation. If an area has too little overlap, the app says so instead of guessing.
    The Harmonization Lab shows the raw jump at the 2012 sensor transition next to the harmonised series, plus the calibration fit, validation, and a sensitivity analysis. The Methodology page documents every assumption and limitation.

Data and scale
The live deployment includes about 44 million real FIRMS detections: the full 2000–2026 history for Europe, North America, and Argentina, plus global coverage for 2026. The server adds the newest Near Real-Time detections from the FIRMS API every 3 hours. No simulated data is used.

Benefits
A consistent record lets fire managers see which months and years burned the most, compare a current fire season with the past, and plan monitoring for critical periods without being misled by a satellite change. Because MODIS is nearing the end of its life, harmonisation keeps 25 years of history usable in the VIIRS era.

What we hope to achieve next
Validate against independent burned-area products (MODIS MCD64A1, EFFIS); add ESA Copernicus Sentinel-3 SLSTR active fires as a third sensor; extend the full history to the whole globe; and add alerts for areas that enter an anomalous period.

Tools
Python (FastAPI, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Shapely, ReportLab); TypeScript (React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for the 3D globe, Recharts); Docker, Caddy, and Google Cloud for hosting. Code: https://github.com/pragatibhandari/firescope (MIT license).
